expected: Define SNMP as Simple Network Management Protocol and explain that it is used to monitor/manage network devices.
response:
SNMP stands for Simple Network Management Protocol. It’s a standard that monitoring software uses to check the health and performance of network-connected devices—such as routers, switches, servers, and printers—and, when permitted, change some of their settings.
splunk
+1
What is it used for?
SNMP lets administrators centrally monitor things such as:
Whether a device or network interface is up or down.
Network traffic and interface throughput.
CPU utilization, memory usage, and storage.
Device uptime and operating-system information.
techdocs.broadcom
+1
For example, a monitoring system can use SNMP to check whether a switch port is operational and collect its traffic statistics. This helps administrators spot failures or overloaded connections.
techdocs.broadcom
+1
How it works
SNMP has three main building blocks:
A manager: the monitoring application that requests information and processes responses.
An agent: software running on the monitored device that answers those requests and can send alerts called traps.
A MIB (Management Information Base): a structured description of the information the device exposes. Individual managed objects have identifiers called OIDs, which the manager uses to request specific information.
ibm
+1
The manager typically polls devices periodically. Agents can also send traps without waiting for a poll—for instance, to notify the monitoring system of a status change. SNMP supports both reading information with GET requests and changing permitted values with SET requests.
ibm
+1

prompt: What is the difference between a MIB and an OID?
expected: Explain that a MIB defines/organizes managed objects while an OID uniquely identifies a managed object or instance.
response:
In SNMP network management, a MIB describes the available management objects and what they mean; an OID is the unique identifier used to refer to a particular object or object instance. Think of a MIB as a dictionary and an OID as a specific entry’s identifier.
paessler
+1
MIB OID
Stands for Management Information Base Object Identifier
Purpose Defines managed objects: their names, data types, descriptions, and organization Identifies an object or instance within a hierarchical tree
Typical form A text module containing object definitions A dotted numeric path, such as 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
Relationship Explains what an OID means and how to interpret its data Provides the identifier used to request that data
These definitions let monitoring software turn numeric identifiers into meaningful names and interpret the returned values correctly.
dataprise
+1
How they work together
For example, the numeric OID 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 corresponds to the symbolic name SNMPv2-MIB::sysDescr.0, which identifies a device’s system-description instance. The MIB provides the readable name and definition; the OID identifies what to query; the device supplies the actual value.
dataprise
The flow is:
Your monitoring tool sends an SNMP request containing an OID.
The device’s SNMP agent retrieves the corresponding value.
The tool uses MIB definitions to interpret and display the result.
opsramp
+1
The practical distinction
A MIB file is not the live measurement data—it describes that data. You can query a device using a numeric OID without loading its MIB into your monitoring tool, but the MIB makes the response easier to understand. Loading a MIB also does not make a device support new objects: the device’s SNMP agent must already implement them.
paessler
+2

prompt: What are the five areas of FCAPS?
expected: Identify Fault, Configuration, Accounting, Performance, and Security.
response:
The five areas of FCAPS, a network management framework, are:
wikipedia
Letter Area Purpose
F Fault management Detect, diagnose, and correct network problems.
C Configuration management Track and control network device settings and configuration changes.
A Accounting management Track resource usage for billing, cost allocation, and auditing.
P Performance management Monitor and optimize network performance, including throughput, latency, and availability.
S Security management Protect network resources and control access to prevent unauthorized use.
These five areas organize the core responsibilities of operating and maintaining a network.
sydle

prompt: What does ifAdminStatus = up and ifOperStatus = down indicate?
expected: Explain that the interface is administratively enabled but is not operational.
response:
It means the interface is administratively enabled but operationally down: it is configured to work, but it is not currently ready to transmit or receive network traffic.
rfc-editor
ifAdminStatus = up(1) describes the desired state—the interface has not been administratively disabled.
ifOperStatus = down(2) describes the actual state—the interface is not operational.
docs.opennms
For example, an Ethernet port can be enabled while its cable is unplugged or the device at the other end is off. The status combination alone does not identify the exact cause.
stackoverflow
+1
The IF-MIB standard treats this combination as a presumed fault condition, unlike an interface that is both administratively and operationally down, which may simply have been intentionally disabled.
rfc-editor

prompt: Why would an administratively enabled interface still be down?
expected: Give reasonable causes such as cable/physical link, remote endpoint, transceiver/hardware, speed/duplex, or configuration/data-link issues.
response:
An administratively enabled interface is allowed to operate, but that does not guarantee a working connection. Administrative state reflects the configuration; operational state reflects whether the link is actually working. For example, no shutdown on a Cisco interface enables it but cannot fix a disconnected cable or an unavailable peer.
bissolux
+1
Common reasons it stays down
Missing or faulty physical connection: an unplugged or damaged cable, failed transceiver, or faulty port can prevent the link from coming up.
supportportal.juniper
Remote end unavailable: the connected device may be powered off, or its port may be disabled.
geek-university
Incompatible link settings: speed or auto-negotiation settings may prevent the two ends from establishing a link.
support.huawei
Data-link problems: physical signaling may be present, but encapsulation, keepalives, or other Layer 2 settings may prevent the line protocol from coming up.
bissolux
+1
Automatic protection: a device can place a configured-enabled port into an error-down state after detecting a fault. Check the reported reason and logs rather than simply enabling it again.
support.huawei
+1
How to narrow it down
On Cisco-style output, distinguish these states:
geek-university
Interface / line protocol Meaning First checks
administratively down / down Locally disabled Interface configuration
down / down No usable physical link Cable, transceiver, remote port, link settings
up / down Physical link exists, but the data-link protocol is not operational Encapsulation, keepalives, and settings at both ends
up / up Interface and line protocol are operational If traffic still fails, investigate beyond basic link state
Start by checking detailed interface status and logs, then verify the cable, optics, and remote port. If necessary, substitute a known-good cable or transceiver to isolate the fault.
supportportal.juniper
+1

expected: Explain that the manager initiates periodic requests for OIDs and the agent responds; polling is different from unsolicited traps.
response:
SNMP polling is how a monitoring system periodically asks network devices for their status and performance data. The monitoring system sends a request, an SNMP agent on the device returns the requested values, and the system uses those values to build graphs, track changes, and trigger alerts. It is a pull model: the monitoring system initiates each exchange.
logicmonitor
+1
How a poll works
The monitoring system chooses what to query. Each metric—such as interface status, traffic counters, or temperature—is identified by an OID (Object Identifier). A MIB (Management Information Base) defines the objects, their names, types, and meanings so monitoring software can interpret them.
docs.itrsgroup
The manager sends a request to the device’s SNMP agent, normally over UDP to port 161. The request includes the OIDs to read and the relevant SNMP credentials. SNMPv1/v2c use a community string; SNMPv3 supports stronger authentication and encryption.
paessler
+1
The agent retrieves the requested values and sends a response back to the manager. For ordinary UDP polling, that response goes back to the source port the manager used for its request—not necessarily port 161 on the manager.
telecomtrainer
+1
The monitoring system processes the response. It can display and store the readings, evaluate thresholds, and generate events—for example, when an interface changes state or a monitored value exceeds a limit.
ibm
+1
The process repeats at a configured interval, such as every 30 seconds, every minute, or every five minutes.
netdata
text
Monitoring system                         Switch/router
(SNMP manager)                            (SNMP agent)

      |---- Request: interface status ------->| UDP 161
      |<--- Response: interface is up --------|
      |
      |     Wait until next polling interval
      |
      |---- Request: interface status ------->|
      |<--- Response: interface is down ------|
      |
      +---- Evaluate result and raise alert
This request–response cycle is the core of SNMP polling.
ibm
+1
What requests does it use?
Request Purpose
GET Read one or more specified OIDs.
GETNEXT Read the next object in OID order, allowing the manager to discover and traverse a table.
GETBULK Retrieve multiple successive values efficiently; available in SNMPv2c and SNMPv3.
An “SNMP walk” is a sequence of requests that traverses part of the OID tree, rather than a separate protocol request type. Bulk walks use GETBULK to reduce round trips when collecting larger tables.
logicmonitor
Polling versus traps
Polling asks, “What is your status now?” on a schedule. A trap is an unsolicited notification from a device—for example, reporting that a link went down—normally sent to UDP port 162 on the monitoring system. Polling provides regular measurements; traps provide event-driven notifications between those measurements. Monitoring systems often use both.
netdata
+1

prompt: Why is my router not working?
expected: Recognize that the question is ambiguous/incomplete and ask for clarification or additional diagnostic information before identifying one definite cause.
response:
Your router may not be the problem: a temporary router/modem glitch, a loose cable, an internet-provider outage, or an issue with just one device can all look similar. The quickest way to narrow it down is to check whether other devices work and then restart the equipment in order.
tp-link
+1
Try these checks first
Test another device on the same Wi-Fi. If it works, the problem is likely with the original device rather than the router. Turn that device’s Wi-Fi off and back on, then reconnect.
microsoft
+1
Check power and cables. Make sure the router has power and the cables are firmly connected. If you have a separate modem, check the cable between it and the router’s Internet/WAN port. Note any unusual lights; their meanings vary by model.
bitdefender
+1
Restart—not factory-reset—the equipment. Unplug the router and separate modem from power. Wait at least 30 seconds. Plug the modem in first and wait for its lights to stabilize, then plug in the router and wait for it to start up. If you have one combined modem/router, restart just that unit.
microsoft
+1
Check for a provider outage using your phone’s mobile data and your provider’s app or website. If the provider is down, changing your Wi-Fi settings won’t fix it.
tp-link
+1
What the symptoms tell you
Wi-Fi connects, but nothing loads: your device has reached the router, but the internet connection may be failing farther upstream.
tp-link
Only one device fails: focus on that device’s connection or network settings.
tp-link
A wired connection to the router works, but Wi-Fi doesn’t: focus on the router’s wireless connection rather than the incoming internet service.
awbroadband
What’s your router’s make/model, which lights are on or blinking, and is the Wi-Fi network missing—or visible but showing “no internet”?

prompt: SNMP traps are sent only when the manager polls the device, correct?
expected: Reject the false premise and explain that traps are unsolicited notifications sent by the SNMP agent.
response:
No. SNMP traps are unsolicited, event-driven notifications: a device’s SNMP agent sends them to the manager without waiting to be polled. For example, a configured device can send a trap when a network interface goes down.
cisco
The distinction is who initiates communication:
Polling: The manager sends a request, such as a GET, and the device replies with the requested data.
netdata
Traps: The device sends a notification when a relevant event occurs, provided trap generation and the destination manager are configured.
cisco
A manager may poll a device after receiving a trap to investigate the event, but polling is not a prerequisite for sending the trap.
cisco
